fixes.explanation: Yes, and Israel answers with a question. The LORD says He has loved them, and they ask, “How have You loved us?” (Malachi 1:2) That's a real question from the people, right in the middle of the LORD's words. I think they wanted Him to show them.

Jacob it is. The LORD says, “Yet Jacob I have loved…” (Malachi 1:2) Jacob is the one God later renamed Israel (Genesis 35:10), so the LORD is talking to Jacob's own family line. That's why the brothers come up when He answers their question.

Wasteland is the word. The LORD says, “…I have made his mountains a wasteland and left his inheritance to the desert jackals.” (Malachi 1:3) Mountains that should be solid and lasting, and the jackals get the inheritance. That's a hard picture to look at.

A garden would be a nice change, baker, but that's not what the LORD says. He says He made Esau's mountains “a wasteland,” and the inheritance went to the desert jackals. (Malachi 1:3) Desert jackals and a garden don't sound like the same neighborhood to me.

A fortress sounds strong, but that's the opposite of this verse. The LORD says He made Esau's mountains “a wasteland” and left his inheritance to the desert jackals. (Malachi 1:3) I bet that's a long way from a fortress.

That's it. The LORD of Hosts says, “They may build, but I will demolish.” (Malachi 1:4) Edom, the people who came from Esau (Genesis 36:8-9), has plans to rebuild, but the LORD says what He will do about them. Rebuilding is a lot of work, and I wouldn't want to hear that part.

I love the hopeful thinking, friend, but the LORD says the opposite. His words are, “They may build, but I will demolish.” (Malachi 1:4) Edom, the people who came from Esau (Genesis 36:8-9), gets no building help here.

Yes, and what a line. The LORD says Israel will see this with their own eyes and say, “The LORD is great—even beyond the borders of Israel.” (Malachi 1:5) They won't just hear about it, they'll see it for themselves. Friend, that's a big sentence about a big God.
